item.title: “Monks, whatever is greed — that is unwholesome. Whatever a person does bodily, verbally, or mentally with greed — that is unwholesome. When a person…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is greed — that is unwholesome. Whatever a person does bodily, verbally, or mentally with greed — that is unwholesome. When a person with greed, overcome by greed, with mind uncontrolled, makes another suffer — by killing, binding, confiscation, abuse, or expulsion — thinking ‘I am strong, I have power’ — that is unwholesome. Thus, many evil, unwholesome states arise in him born of greed, originating from greed, produced by greed.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.69
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with…
item.description:
“Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, there is knowledge: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.15

item.title: The hair is curled in seven rings, The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge — Enough to fool a fool, But not one who…
item.description:
The hair is curled in seven rings,
The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - “Wonderful, Venerable Bharadvāja! Marvelous, Venerable Bharadvāja! This is well spoken by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.…
item.description:
- “Wonderful, Venerable Bharadvāja! Marvelous, Venerable Bharadvāja! This is well spoken by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. This very cause, this very reason, Venerable Bharadvāja, is why these young monks, youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, do not indulge in sensual pleasures and live the perfectly pure holy life for their whole life, completing it fully. I too, Venerable Bharadvāja, when I enter the inner apartments with body unguarded, speech unguarded, mind unguarded, mindfulness unestablished, sense faculties unrestrained — then lust overcomes me. But, Venerable Bharadvāja, when I enter the inner apartments with body guarded, speech guarded, mind guarded, mindfulness established, sense faculties restrained — then lust does not overcome me.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.127
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Here, brahmin, a person is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not…
item.description:
“Here, brahmin, a person is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, not free from craving. Then a severe illness arises for him. Affected by that severe illness, he thinks: ‘Truly, agreeable sensual pleasures will leave me,’ or ‘I will leave agreeable sensual pleasures.’ He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. This, brahmin, is a person who is subject to death, fearful, and falls into terror at the thought of death.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.184
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - What binds the world? What leads the world? By abandoning what thing Is Nibbāna called? - Delight binds the world, Seeking leads the world,…
item.description:
- What binds the world?
What leads the world?
By abandoning what thing
Is Nibbāna called?
- Delight binds the world,
Seeking leads the world,
By abandoning craving,
Is Nibbāna called.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.64
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - What hangs up the world? What envelops the world? What closes in the world? Upon what does the world stand? - Craving hangs up…
item.description:
- What hangs up the world?
What envelops the world?
What closes in the world?
Upon what does the world stand?
- Craving hangs up the world,
Aging envelops the world,
Death closes in the world,
Upon suffering the world stands.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.67
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, through lust, one is not freed. Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form…
item.description:
“Monks, through lust, one is not freed. Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Through lust for feeling … for perception … for formations, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With formations as its object, with formations as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Monks, if anyone says: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will show the coming and going, the passing away and arising, the growth, increase, and expansion of consciousness’ — such a thing is not possible. Monks, if a monk has abandoned lust for the form element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. If a monk has abandoned lust for the feeling element … for the perception element … for the formation element … Monks, if a monk has abandoned lust for the consciousness element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. Without that support, consciousness does not expand, does not generate activity, and is liberated. Being liberated, it is steady; being steady, it is content; being content, it is not agitated; being not agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.53
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached…
item.description:
“Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached to form. If there were no peril in form, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because there is peril in form, beings become disenchanted with form. And, monks, as long as beings do not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, and the escape as escape in regard to these five aggregates of clinging, they have not, monks, escaped from this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans; they are not free from it, not detached, not liberated, their minds are not at ease. But when they directly know these five aggregates … as they actually are, then they have escaped … their minds are at ease.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.28
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing.…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Sounds cognizable by the ear … Odors cognizable by the nose … Tastes cognizable by the tongue … Tangibles cognizable by the body—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
